title: What should you ask first in an investment or capacity case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in an investment or capacity case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Ask first whether the demand is real and lasting, and whether existing capacity can be squeezed harder, before you discuss building anything. The trap is approving a big capital spend before fixing bottlenecks and comparing cheaper alternatives such as outsourcing or leasing.
body:
The first question to ask

Is the demand real and lasting, and can we get more out of what we already have?

An investment case usually arrives framed as "should we build it?" The best first move is to test the need. A demand forecast built on one strong year, or on a single big customer, is a weak reason to spend millions. And many operations have hidden capacity: a slow step that limits the whole line, long changeovers, or a second shift that is not running. Ask what is driving the forecast and how close current assets are to their real limit.

How to build your structure

  • Need: is the demand real and lasting; can existing capacity be squeezed first?
  • Economics: upfront and running cost, extra margin, payback, and what happens to prices if rivals add capacity too.
  • Alternatives: outsource, lease, subcontract, or shift work between sites.
  • Execution: time to build, skills, risks.

The full tree is in the investment decision framework.

Turn demand growth into a capacity decision

A factory can make 1 million units a year and runs at 95%, or 950,000 units. Allowing for maintenance and changeovers, that is close to its practical limit. Demand is forecast to rise to 1.2 million, a gap of 250,000 units.

Option A: build a new line

A new line adds 300,000 units of capacity for $4M upfront and $600k a year to run. Each unit sold contributes $5 before the line's own costs.

  • Extra contribution: 250,000 × $5 = $1.25M
  • Less running cost: $1.25M − $600k = $650k a year
  • Simple payback: $4M ÷ $650k ≈ 6.2 years (before tax, financing and working capital)

Option B: use a contract manufacturer

Suppose a contractor makes the extra units for $3 more each than in-house production, so each earns $2 instead of $5. That gives 250,000 × $2 = $500k a year, with no upfront spend.

Compare

The new line earns $150k a year more than outsourcing, for $4M of investment: about 27 years to pay back the difference. Unless demand keeps growing, outsourcing wins. If demand fills the whole 300,000 units, the line's profit rises to $900k ($1.5M − $600k) and payback falls to about 4.4 years, so the forecast is the swing factor. For how to discount these cash flows properly, see payback and NPV worked examples.

The trap most people fall into

Approving capex before fixing bottlenecks or pricing the alternatives. "Demand exceeds capacity, so build" skips every cheaper answer: overtime, removing a bottleneck, contract manufacturing, or turning away low-margin orders.

Weak: "Demand will be above capacity, so they should build the new line."
Strong: "At 250,000 extra units, outsourcing earns $500k a year with no investment, against $650k for a $4M line. I'd outsource now and build only if demand looks set to pass 1.2 million."

For a structured way to make that call, see outsource or keep in-house.

Two prompts to try

Should a UK university open a campus in Singapore?

Show the answer
  • Demand: students in the region and what they will pay; competition from local and other foreign universities.
  • Economics: set-up cost, fees, staff; break-even student numbers.
  • Quality and brand: teaching and degrees equal to the home campus; risk to reputation.
  • Regulation and partners: local approvals; partner or go alone.

Where to start: demand. Will enough students pay fees close to UK levels to study in Singapore?

The trap: assuming home demand carries over to a new market.

Should a delivery company switch its 2,000 vans to electric?

Show the answer
  • Cost per mile: van price, energy, maintenance; resale value and grants.
  • Operations: range against daily routes; charging at depots and time to charge.
  • Investment and timing: upfront cost and financing; switch all now, or as old vans retire.
  • Other benefits and risks: clean-air zones, customer demands; battery life, depot grid capacity.

Where to start: total cost per mile over a van's life, not the purchase price.

The trap: comparing only purchase prices.

Where to practise next

Try Desert Dairy, a dairy deciding whether to build a new plant, and BlueTide Seafood, own the trucks or keep paying a logistics firm. Then work through the investment structuring practice set.
